LESSON 17 OF 106·Network Attacks and Defences

Eavesdropping: Why Traffic Is Readable in the Clear

Why unencrypted traffic can be read by anyone on the path, what an eavesdropper actually learns, and how encryption in transit removes the whole class of attack.

Beginner12 min
Why this matters

Traffic on a shared network is readable unless it is encrypted, and most internal traffic historically was not. Understanding what an observer can learn from unencrypted traffic is the basis for deciding what must be encrypted.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • On a hub, or any segment where traffic is broadcast, a device can read frames not addressed to it without doing anything unusual.
  • A switched network forwards each frame only to the right port, so ordinary eavesdropping needs either the switch to be coerced or the traffic to be routed through an attacker.
  • Any router along the path necessarily sees the packet headers in the clear, because it has to read them to forward the packet.
  • Unencrypted application protocols therefore expose their contents, including credentials sent in a request body or a cookie.
  • TLS removes that exposure for the part of the path it covers, which is why the endpoints matter as much as the protocol.

The background

  • Shared-medium Ethernet made passive listening trivial, and the switch was partly a performance feature before it became a security boundary.
  • Wired equivalent privacy and similar link-layer protections addressed wireless eavesdropping but not traffic on the wire itself.
  • As protocols moved to TLS by default, passive interception became much harder and attackers shifted to endpoints and to plaintext services that remained.
  • Certificate transparency and pinning were added to close the gap where a trusted authority issued a certificate for someone else name.

Real-world examples

  • A legacy service that still speaks a plaintext protocol exposes its traffic even on a fully switched network.
  • Email submitted without transport encryption reveals message content to anyone on the path, which is why mail servers are configured to upgrade.
  • A device on the same wireless network as a misconfigured service can read that service traffic directly.

What to look for

  • Identify any protocol on your network that still sends secrets in the clear, including within an internal segment.
  • Check that a switch is actually managed, since an unmanaged device forwards everywhere.
  • Confirm that management protocols such as telnet are replaced by their encrypted equivalents.
  • Treat a router or proxy in the path as able to read anything not encrypted end to end.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Require encryption for every protocol that carries authentication or personal data, including legacy ones.
  • Replace plaintext management protocols with SSH, and plaintext mail submission with an encrypted one.
  • Use managed switches and disable unused ports so a device cannot listen passively on a shared segment.
  • Encrypt traffic end to end where the endpoints are trusted, rather than only between hops.
